description: examples/fullstack/main.go hardcodes SecretKey "replace-with-a-32-byte-minimum-secret-in-production!" (52 bytes, passes the 32-byte MinSecretKeyLength gate) and docs/content/docs/sdk/tokens-and-http.md publishes SecretKey "super-secret-32-byte-key-here!!!" (exactly 32 bytes, passes the gate). Both strings are public on GitHub, so any deployment that copy-pastes the example/docs without replacing the key mints HS256 tokens with an attacker-known key: the attacker replays the published string into their own jwt.New instance and forges access tokens the victim verifies. PoC test proves cross-instance forgery for both literals. Mitigating context: both sites carry replace-me comments and the library itself panics on short keys (TASK-067) — the gap is that a syntactically valid, publicly-known key is indistinguishable from a real one at construction.
remediation: Replace both literals with a crypto/rand generation snippet (e.g. `key := make([]byte, 32); rand.Read(key)` plus hex/base64 encode) and a warning that the value must come from a secret manager; never publish a valid-length key. Consider adding a denylist in jwt.New/Validate rejecting these exact published strings so copy-paste deployments fail fast. Docs example should use an obviously-invalid placeholder (e.g. <32 bytes) or os.Getenv pattern so pasted code refuses to boot.
title: Published valid-length HS256 signing keys in example and docs enable token forgery on copy-paste deployments

description: examples/fullstack/main.go builds the passkey ceremony-cookie HMAC key as `make([]byte, 32)` — 32 zero bytes, which passes the MinCookieKeyLength (32) gate and is known to every repo reader (PoC proves NewService accepts it). docs/content/docs/sdk/mfa.md publishes `[]byte("very-secure-32-byte-secret-key!!")` (exactly 32 bytes, passes the gate). A deployment copying either value HMACs ceremony cookies with an attacker-known key, letting the attacker forge ceremony-cookie state (challenge binding) that the server trusts. PoC proves both keys are accepted by passkey.NewService. Mitigating context: the example carries a 'replace with crypto/rand in production' comment and the failure mode requires copy-paste deployment; the ceremony still requires a real WebAuthn ceremony, bounding impact to ceremony-state forgery rather than direct authentication.
remediation: Replace the zero-key line with a crypto/rand generation snippet and a fail-fast guard (reject all-zero keys at NewService construction, e.g. compare against zero buffer); replace the docs literal with a generation snippet plus secret-manager guidance. Add the published docs string to a denylist so pasted deployments fail closed.
title: Attacker-known passkey ceremony-cookie HMAC keys in example and docs

description: The default identity LoginHandler maps ErrAccountLocked and ErrAccountDisabled to HTTP 429 "account_locked" while unknown identifiers and wrong passwords map to 401 "invalid_credentials" (identity/handlers.go mapAuthError, uniformAuthErrors=false by default). An unauthenticated attacker therefore learns account existence: (a) a disabled account answers 429 on the very first attempt vs 401 for unknown; (b) after N failed logins a real account flips to 429 while an unknown identifier stays 401 forever. This undercuts the service layer's decoy-hash anti-enumeration work at the HTTP boundary, and ships in the default webapp preset (webapp never sets WithUniformAuthErrors). PoC tests demonstrate both oracles end-to-end at the handler layer. [Also flagged independently as IE-01 by the input-exposure agent, which proved the single-shot disabled-vs-unknown variant at the handler layer.]
remediation: Fail closed by default: make uniform 401 "invalid_credentials" the default in newHandlerConfig (keep a distinct opt-in, e.g. WithVerboseLockoutStatus, for deployments that accept the oracle for UX), or set WithUniformAuthErrors() in the webapp preset. Concrete change: identity/handlers.go — default uniformAuthErrors=true; webapp/webapp.go — append identity.WithUniformAuthErrors() to idOpts.
title: Login status oracle: locked/disabled accounts answer 429 vs 401 by default (account enumeration)

description: mfa.StepUpHandler re-issues the full access+refresh pair after a valid second factor but only propagates Claims.MustChangePassword when the host wires WithMustChangeResolver (mfa/handlers.go:450, nil by default). The interim token minted by identity.LoginHandler's MFA gate DOES carry the flag, so a must-change, MFA-enrolled user who completes step-up on default wiring receives a fresh refresh family with flag=false; Rotate then replays false on every silent refresh and WithPasswordChangeGate stops diverting. With the default MaxRefreshLifetime=0 (unbounded family lifetime) the evasion persists indefinitely; only the next interactive login re-flags (LoginHandler re-checks PasswordChangeRequired). PoC completes a real recovery-code step-up behind ContextMiddleware and shows the stepped-up JWT lost the flag, while the resolver-wired variant preserves it.
remediation: Preserve by default instead of opt-in: in mfa.StepUpHandler, default the must-change decision to the interim token's verified claims (tokens.ClaimsFromContext[C](r.Context())) when mustChangeResolve is nil, i.e. treat a flagged interim as flagged unless explicitly overridden. Concrete change: mfa/handlers.go StepUpHandler — `if cfg.mustChangeResolve != nil ? cfg.mustChangeResolve(r) : interimMustChangeFromContext(r)` where the fallback reads ClaimsFromContext[C]. Keep WithMustChangeResolver as an override, and document that custom StepUpClaimsBuilders must re-check identity.PasswordChangeRequired.
title: MFA step-up drops MustChangePassword by default (forced-password-change bypass)

description: identity.RequestMagicLink and identity.RequestPasswordReset mint single-use tokens for administratively DISABLED accounts (memory and pgx CreateVerificationToken gate only on DeletedAt, never DisabledAt) and return them to the caller for delivery, while unknown identifiers yield ("", nil, nil). The shipped handlers mask this with a uniform 204, but Service-API consumers that branch on the token/user return (or on mailer invocation) get a liveness signal, and suspended users keep receiving credential emails. The consume-time gate (consumeForLiveUser rejects DisabledAt) only fires later, after delivery. PoC shows non-empty tokens minted for a disabled account vs empty for unknown, and that the reset token is still correctly rejected at consume time.
remediation: Enforce the disabled check at mint time, mirroring consumeForLiveUser: in RequestMagicLink/RequestPasswordReset/RequestPasswordResetViaRecovery (and RequestEmailVerification), return ("", nil, nil) after a decoyToken() when the resolved user has DisabledAt set. Concrete change: identity/service.go — after FindUserByEmail success, `if user.DisabledAt != nil { s.decoyToken(); return "", nil, nil }`. Optionally extend the pgx/memory CreateVerificationToken EXISTS guards with `AND disabled_at IS NULL` as defense-in-depth.
title: Password-reset / magic-link tokens minted for disabled accounts (issuance-time liveness gap)

description: The OAuth state cookie (default name "oauth_state", no __Host- prefix) carries the CSRF state + PKCE verifier + nonce + provider + tenant with HMAC integrity ONLY when the host sets WithStateSigningKey; otherwise packState/unpackState accept any well-formed 5-field value (oauth/state.go, oauth/handlers.go). An attacker able to plant cookies (sibling-subdomain tossing — the auth cookies are __Host- protected but the state cookie is not) can forge a state cookie without a Begin round trip and pair it with their own authorization-response link, driving the victim's browser through CallbackHandler into a session bound to the attacker's linked identity (login CSRF). State-cookie HMAC signing alone would not stop a Begin-capable attacker either; the missing control is browser-key binding (e.g. __Host- prefix). PoC proves unsigned forged cookies verify and signed mode rejects them. [Also flagged independently as WEB-01 by the web agent, which proved a self-minted cookie reaches token exchange/issuance without a signing key while the signed-mode control rejects it.]
remediation: Harden the state cookie by default: (1) default the state cookie name to a __Host- prefixed value and validate Secure/no-Domain/Path=/ like tokens.Cookies.Validate does; (2) warn (or fail) when WithStateSigningKey is unset in non-test builds — concrete change: oauth/handlers.go newHandlerConfig + a startup Validate() on handlerConfig mirroring tokens.Cookies.Validate. Document that cross-subdomain deployments needing a shared state cookie must explicitly opt out and accept the login-CSRF residual. Fail closed or warn loudly when no state signing key is configured: require WithStateSigningKey (or derive it from the tenant keystore) for production use, emit a startup/misuse event when unsigned, and consider a __Host- prefixed default state-cookie name so shared-Domain deployments stay host-locked. At minimum, document that WithCookieDomain + unsigned state cookies re-opens login-CSRF/provider-confusion via subdomain cookie-tossing.
title: OAuth state cookie unsigned and not host-locked by default (login-CSRF craftability)

description: When neither oauth.WithRedirectURL nor oauth.WithAllowedHosts is set, handlerConfig.resolveRedirectURL (oauth/handlers.go) builds redirect_uri as requestScheme(r)+'://'+r.Host+r.URL.Path, where requestScheme trusts the spoofable X-Forwarded-Proto header and r.Host is the raw Host header (isValidHost only checks syntax). The resulting attacker-influenced redirect_uri is sent to the provider in AuthCodeURL and reused in the code exchange. Exploitation additionally requires the provider to honor an unregistered redirect_uri (most strict providers reject it, which bounds severity to Low), plus a Host-poisoning primitive (misbehaving proxy) or a victim clicking a link whose Host the attacker controls at the network edge. PoC (worktree, httptest only): BeginHandler with no redirect/allowlist options and Host 'evil.example' + X-Forwarded-Proto 'https' emits a 302 whose redirect_uri starts with 'https://evil.example/'; the same request with WithAllowedHosts('app.example.com') is rejected 400.
remediation: Require an explicit redirect_uri (WithRedirectURL) or allowlist (WithAllowedHosts) in production: log/emit a misuse event when falling back to Host-derived redirect_uri, never trust X-Forwarded-Proto unless the deployment declares a trusted proxy, and document that the Host-derived fallback is dev-only. Consider rejecting the fallback outright when the request is not loopback/TLS.
title: redirect_uri derived from raw Host + spoofable X-Forwarded-Proto when unconfigured

description: The govulncheck CI job (.github/workflows/ci.yml, job 'govulncheck') scans the core module (GOWORK=off, ./...) and adapters/pgx, but the third Go module adapters/otel (module github.com/JLugagne/egauth/adapters/otel, with direct third-party dependencies go.opentelemetry.io/otel, otel/sdk, otel/trace v1.46.0) has no govulncheck step: the test-adapters-otel job runs only go vet + go test. A known CVE in the OpenTelemetry SDK (or its transitive deps) would therefore not fail CI. Static proof, no PoC test applicable to a pure workflow-coverage gap (poc_test_path null).
remediation: Add a govulncheck step for the otel module mirroring the pgx pattern (working-directory: adapters/otel, `go run golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@v1.1.4 ./...`), or run govulncheck once per module in a matrix over the three module roots.
title: govulncheck does not cover the adapters/otel module
